summary.title: Concurrent Servers: Part 2 - Threads
summary.one_liner: Learn how one-thread-per-client and thread-pool designs handle concurrent network connections, with a pthreads C server and a ThreadPoolExecutor Python server.
keywords: how to handle many clients at once
takeaways: One-thread-per-client servers serve connections concurrently but can exhaust memory and CPU and are vulnerable to DoS.
A thread pool bounds concurrency by design: extra clients wait in a queue until a worker is free.
The C version uses pthread_create and pthread_detach in the accept loop; the Python version uses ThreadPoolExecutor.submit.
Thread pool size should be chosen via benchmarking and the available hardware.
Threads are not the only option; the next part covers event-driven, asynchronous designs.
summary.summary: This is Part 2 of a series on concurrent network servers, building on a sequential baseline from Part 1. It explains the motivation for multithreading (CPU idle time while waiting on network I/O) and presents a one-thread-per-client server in C using pthreads, with thread detachment and a shared serve_connection function. It then discusses the resource and DoS problems of that design and introduces thread pools as a rate-limiting approach, with a Python server using ThreadPoolExecutor and a pool size of 2 to demonstrate queuing behavior via client logs. The post ends by noting threads are one option and previewing event-driven designs in the next part.
